searches.note: Twenty six searches of a share of twenty eight, two left unspent, none of them the author's. Two served the whole group: the Margaret River Wine Association's own domain (the dates of the first five plantings, the research of 1965 and 1966, the trophies of 1983 and 1984) and Wine Australia's (the blending and label rules). Eleven were restricted to a house's own domain (vassefelix.com.au twice, mosswood.com.au twice, cullenwines.com.au four times, leeuwinestate.com.au once, capementelle.com.au once, and decanter.com once for its own Wine Legend) and are read as primary through their summaries; the rest kept the house's domain out so that each second source would be independent. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).
The making and the sites went first to the house's own vintage pages; the history went to the Margaret River Wine Association, Wikipedia, Decanter and the trade with the house's domain kept out.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was found in no source of this check, or in a writer's own site only, it was cut or said with less, and the house's own claims are told as its record.

The dead are named with their dates where two sources agree (Kevin Cullen, 1922 to 1994, by the Australian Dictionary of Biography and Wikipedia; Robert Mondavi, 1913 to 2008, by the refuted napa record), and with the house's own record where it is the founder of that house (Tom Cullity, 1925 to 2008, left open); every living founder, owner, heir and winemaker stays described.

Writers' own sites met among the results (Wine with Seth, Inside Burgundy, The Vintage Journal, An Eye on Wine) are cited neither in the fragment nor as a second source here, though where they disagree with a record they are noted as a reason to say less. The serving temperatures agree with the service reference: full reds 16 to 18 for the four reds, a full white 10 to 13 for the Chardonnay.

tested: Dr Tom Cullity, a Perth cardiologist, founded the estate at Wilyabrup in 1967: the house, Wikipedia, an Aquinas College profile (medicine in 1947) and the Margaret River Wine Association. Confirmed.

His dates, 1925 to 2008: three searches outside the house found no obituary and no death year; his birth in 1925 has the State Library of South Australia by the author's report. Left as the house's record of its founder, and open.

The research of the mid 1960s: the association gives two reports by the agronomist, of 1965 and 1966, as the catalyst of commercial planting; the likeness to Bordeaux rests on the Codex's region record. Confirmed as written.
The first modern commercial vineyard, planted with Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec: the association's own words and the house's. Confirmed, and the record now says modern, as the association does.

The first wines of 1972, a Cabernet Sauvignon Malbec and a Riesling, the region's first serious wines by the house: the house's story page. Confirmed; a writer quoted on the house's site has a 1971 Cabernet that met a spectacular end, so the record keeps 1972 and says nothing of 1971.

The sale of 1984 to a couple by the house, 1985 by another account, and the family that has guided it since 1987: the house and a second profile. Confirmed; the record keeps the mid 1980s and now describes the family of 1987.

The Home Vineyard: the house names the founder's old Houghton clone Cabernet blocks on original roots in ancient gravel loam by the Wilyabrup Brook, and a review on its site says dry grown; one plot is being replanted on rootstock. The clay below was found in no source of this check.

The making: the house's page on the 2022 gives hand picking, whole berries in a wild fermentation pumped over several times a day and eighteen months in French barriques. The fermenter split and the time on skins were found nowhere in this check.

Tom Cullity replacing the Heytesbury red from the 2013 vintage, released in May 2017 for the fiftieth year: The Drinks Business (2016), The Real Review and the house. Confirmed; The Drinks Business adds that about half the fruit of the first came from the founder's vines and half from later plantings, and that the Heytesbury name went to the Chardonnay alone.
The label: Wine Australia's rules require at least 85 per cent for a single variety or GI, and two or more varieties named to total 85 per cent in descending order. Confirmed.

Planting of 1971: the house and the association. Confirmed. Merlot and Cabernet Franc in 1976 and Malbec in 1978: the house's pages on the 2022 and its Merlot. Confirmed. On its own roots and dry farmed were found in no source of this check.
The soil: old granite and gravelly sandy loam over lateritic subsoil, the house's viticulture page. The record's order of words was set to the house's.
The daughter in charge from 1989, with Diana Cullen chief winemaker from 1981: the house. Confirmed and the mother's year added.
Biodynamic certification: the vineyard in 2004 and the winery in 2008 on one house page, since 2005 on another, a trial in 2003 on a third. The story keeps the vineyard's 2004.

The name Diana Madeline: a tasting list on the house's own site shows the 2000 still labelled Cabernet Sauvignon Merlot and the 2001 as Diana Madeline, which with the author's Decanter makes the 2001 vintage; the page's address names a living critic, so the record keeps the start of the 2000s, which stays true.

The making: picked on fruit days (the house on the 2022 and the 2024), no added yeast, acid or malolactic culture and ten to ninety nine days on skins by batch (the 2020), fourteen months with 55 per cent new oak in barriques and puncheons (the 2022). Confirmed, but the house's pages name no forest and no flower days.
The Mangan vineyard: plantings of 1995 and 1997 by the house's viticulture page; beside the first was found nowhere.

Wilyabrup a district, not a registered subregion: Wine Australia's committee declined a final determination of Wilyabrup as a GI, and the association says the six areas proposed in 1999 are not GIs. Confirmed.
